The Ridged-eye flounder (Pleuronichthys cornutus) is a commercially valuable pleuronectid flatfish distributed across the coastal waters of East Asia, from southern Japan to the Yellow Sea. Laboratory rearing studies conducted at a stable temperature of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C] have documented that embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring just 10 days [ab = 10 days] after fertilisation. This brief incubation period is consistent with the small egg size characteristic of the species, a reproductive strategy that shifts energetic investment toward fecundity rather than per-offspring provisioning. The newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days before the commencement of exogenous feeding. Field surveys suggest that spawning takes place during the winter and early spring months, likely timed to coincide with peaks in planktonic productivity that support larval survival. The species exhibits a typical pleuronectid life history, with a pelagic larval phase that undergoes dramatic metamorphosis involving migration of one eye to the contralateral side before settlement onto sandy substrates of the continental shelf. This ontogenetic habitat transition marks the beginning of a benthic existence that will characterise the remainder of the juvenile and adult phases.

Following settlement and metamorphosis, juvenile Ridged-eye flounder enter a period of rapid somatic growth that continues until the onset of gonadal maturation. The total length at which puberty commences has been estimated from histologically examined specimens at 12.7 cm [Lp = 12.7 cm], a size that corresponds to an age of roughly two years under typical environmental conditions. Coinciding with this developmental milestone, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 30.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 30.3 grams], reflecting a substantial accumulation of somatic tissue during the preceding juvenile phase. This body mass is sufficient to support the energetic demands of first gametogenesis, which requires the mobilisation of lipid and protein stores. The onset of vitellogenesis in females is regulated by hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis activation and is sensitive to photoperiod and thermal cues. Comparative data from related pleuronectids indicate that the length at maturity observed in P. cornutus is near the lower end of the range for the genus, possibly reflecting adaptation to the relatively productive but seasonally variable waters of its temperate habitat.

Within a cohort, the largest and oldest individuals of Pleuronichthys cornutus attain an ultimate total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], representing the asymptotic size approached after several years of decelerating growth. The corresponding ultimate female wet weight associated with this maximum length is 399 grams [Wwi = 399 grams], derived from length-weight regressions that indicate isometric scaling relationships typical of demersal flatfishes. Females generally achieve larger asymptotic sizes than males, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism common among pleuronectids and attributed to the fecundity advantages of increased body volume for egg production. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild, based on otolith annulus readings from individuals maintained under natural thermal regimes averaging 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C], reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This extended lifespan positions the species as a moderate-lived teleost, with a generation time that buffers population fluctuations against sporadic recruitment failures. Age-structured stock assessments routinely incorporate these longevity estimates to parameterise natural mortality rates and to inform sustainable harvest limits across the species managed fishery zones.

The reproductive biology of the Ridged-eye flounder is characterised by batch spawning over an extended seasonal period, with females releasing multiple clutches of pelagic eggs. The fecundity per spawning event is moderate, with gravid females producing approximately 100,000 to 150,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 100,000 to 150,000 eggs per clutch], reflecting the small egg diameter and the high fecundity typical of many marine flatfishes. Spawning occurs at a frequency of roughly one event every ten to fourteen days [F_R_i = roughly one event every ten to fourteen days] during the peak of the reproductive season, such that the total seasonal egg output can accumulate considerably. The wet weight at birth, derived from the calculated egg volume assuming a spherical diameter of 0.8 mm, is approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams]; this minute initial mass underscores the extreme altriciality of the free-floating embryos, which must rapidly acquire exogenous energy after hatching. Ovarian development follows a group-synchronous pattern, with a reserve of oocytes maturing progressively to replace those released during each successive spawning bout.

Comparative physiological studies have investigated the metabolic scope of Pleuronichthys cornutus in relation to its benthic lifestyle and seasonal temperature fluctuations. Routine oxygen consumption rates in adults are consistent with the relatively sedentary, ambush-feeding habits of flatfishes, which minimise locomotory costs compared to pelagic foragers. At the same thermal regime of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C] used in the developmental studies, the extended maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] documented from field-caught specimens is notably greater than that reported for several sympatric pleuronectids, suggesting a slower life-history pace potentially linked to lower intrinsic mortality rates on the demersal habitat. The total length at puberty of 12.7 cm [Lp = 12.7 cm] represents roughly forty percent of the ultimate total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a proportion that aligns with the general pleuronectid pattern in which reproductive maturity is attained at a moderate fraction of maximum size. This relationship implies a balanced allocation of growth between pre-reproductive and reproductive life stages. Future research investigating the genetic basis of growth variation and its correlation with maturation timing could provide valuable insights for aquaculture broodstock management and for predicting population responses to warming sea temperatures in the species range.
